nodes.title: Task selection is round-robin modulo the unsolved pool, not a bandit, VOI rule, or difficulty target
nodes.body: src/runtime/selector.js:48-55: pickTask filters the eval set to tasks where isSolved(taskId,best) is false (score >= 1), then takes open[(round-1) % open.length]. There is no difficulty term, no cost term, no expected-gain term, no randomness, and no exploration bonus. Two consequences follow mechanically. First, the registration order of the eval set IS the curriculum: index 0 runs in round 1, index 1 in round 2, and nothing about measured outcomes can reorder them. Second, the selector computes poolSize and solvedCount and discards them - no round records why a task was chosen, so selection quality is unattributable after the fact. A second, competing selector exists at src/runtime/sampling.js:31 with the same modulo rule plus a holdoutEvery cadence, but holdoutEvery is null in all 69 real campaigns, so that path never fires. Limitation: this is one repository's code and one 231-round ledger; the ledger cannot separate bad selection from bad candidate generation, because both produce an identical zero-score round.

nodes.title: 43 of 59 multi-task campaigns (72.9%) never attempted at least one task in their own eval set
nodes.body: Over 69 campaigns in C:/Users/Darkness/.dsh/loom/campaigns/*/events.jsonl, ever-attempted rate by registration index collapses: index 0 attempted in 69/69 campaigns (100%), index 1 in 43/59 (72.9%), index 2 in 11/35 (31.4%), index 3 in 1/6 (16.7%). Thirty of 69 campaigns ran fewer rounds than their eval set has tasks (loom-ui: 3 tasks, 0 rounds; loom-holdout-live: 4 tasks, 2 rounds; loom-ab: 2 tasks, 1 round). The mechanism is not adversarial: round-robin advances one task per round, so any campaign that stops after k rounds has touched only the first k tasks, and median rounds per campaign is 2. Coverage is therefore a function of campaign lifetime, not of difficulty. Limitation: this counts attempts, not value; a starved task may be correctly starved, and the early-stop decision that causes starvation is itself unexplained in the ledger, so n is 59 campaigns that mostly ran 1-3 rounds.

nodes.title: 84 of 114 promotions land in a task's first round; only 8 of 40 round-1 failures ever promote
nodes.body: Splitting the 124 (campaign,task) slots by their first round's outcome: 84 slots promoted in round 1 and all 84 of those first rounds promoted; of the 40 slots whose first round failed, only 8 (20%) ever promoted later. Promotions earned in rounds >= 2 total 20, spread across 10 slots (loom-self3/exposure alone promoted in rounds 6,7,8,9). Round-level persistence is equally sharp: P(next round produces a verifying attempt | this round did) = 32/36 = 0.889, versus 9/67 = 0.134 after a failing round. So one round of evidence about a task carries most of the information the loop will ever get about it, and the loop currently spends it by moving to the next index anyway. Limitation: round 1 always picks eval index 0, so first-round success partly encodes 'the index-0 task is the easy one'; this pattern cannot separate task identity from earliness, and a within-task randomised order experiment is missing.

nodes.title: Verify probability falls from 0.69 on a fresh task to 0.04 after three consecutive failures
nodes.body: Conditioning each attempt on the number of immediately preceding consecutive non-verifying attempts on the same (campaign,task) slot: 0 prior failures -> 183/265 = 0.691; 1 -> 26/60 = 0.433; 2 -> 8/31 = 0.258; 3 -> 1/23 = 0.043; 4 -> 1/16 = 0.062; 5 -> 0/15; 6 or more -> 0/42. Overall 219/452 = 0.485, and 102 of 124 slots verify at least once while 22 never do. This is the shape a selector needs: after three failures the expected yield of another pull is near zero and the correct action is to reallocate, which round-robin cannot express. Limitation: the hazard is conditional on observed failures only - attempts abandoned before finishing, and the 127 attempts (28% of 452) that errored, are not counted as failures here; and the loop may have been lowering its own patch quality as budget ran down, so the collapse may be campaign fatigue wearing a task-difficulty costume rather than a property of the task.

nodes.title: Re-attempt decay tracks repetition count, not eval-set position - and is confounded with campaign age
nodes.body: Two cross-tabs on the same 452 attempts. By repeat index (nth round on that campaign+task): 0 -> 152/247 = 0.615, 1 -> 35/95 = 0.368, 2 -> 16/48 = 0.333, 3 -> 6/28 = 0.214, 4 -> 10/34 = 0.294. By registration index: 0 -> 115/242 = 0.475, 1 -> 69/148 = 0.466, 2 -> 24/46 = 0.522, 3 -> 8/10 = 0.800. There is no monotone difficulty gradient by position, so registration order is not a hidden difficulty prior; the only monotone signal is that repeating a task gets worse. That is the empirical case for a discard rule and against an easy-to-hard ordering, and it also means a bandit's job here is mostly retiring arms, not ranking them. Limitation: repeat index and campaign age are collinear under round-robin (the 5th round on a slot is also a late campaign round), so this cannot distinguish task saturation from budget exhaustion, and 23 interrupted rounds plus 127 errored attempts sit inside the same window.

nodes.title: Per-task pass rates are bimodal: 22 slots never verify and 51 always do, out of 124 slots
nodes.body: Across the 124 slots with at least two attempts, 22 have an all-fail rate (0.0) and 51 an all-pass rate (1.0); the remaining 51 sit in between but are thinly sampled (attempts per slot: 2 on 77 slots, 4 on 23, 6 on 10, 8 on 5, 10+ on 9). The 32 slots that never promoted consumed 108 of 227 rounds, 47.6% of all rounds. Because the verifier is binary, a hard task and an impossible task produce the same observation until someone runs the counterfactual, which the loop never does. Bayesian arm models do not rescue this: Beta(1,9) versus Beta(9,1) is exactly re-discovering the mode, and with 2-6 pulls per arm the posterior on a genuinely 0.4 task is indistinguishable from the posterior on a 0.05 task. Limitation: with a median of 2 attempts per slot the middle of the distribution is unobservable by construction, so bimodality is partly a measurement artefact of tiny n rather than a property of the task population.

nodes.title: Retiring a task after one non-promoted round would skip 91 of 231 rounds and 31% of round spend
nodes.body: Replaying three retirement rules over the same ledger: retire after K consecutive non-promoted rounds. K=1 skips 91 of 231 rounds ($0.034 of $0.108 round spend); K=2 skips 53 ($0.0186); K=3 skips 29 ($0.0093). Cost per verified attempt is $0.00049 over 452 attempts. Separately, 108 of 231 rounds (46.8%) occur after the campaign's last promotion and cost $0.0465 plus 5.47 wall-clock hours - so 'retire the campaign' and 'retire the task' are large and partly overlapping savings. The K=1 number is the aggressive end: because 84 of 114 promotions are first-round promotions, one non-promoted round is already a 0.8-probability signal of no future promotion. Limitation: this is a replay on the ledger that generated the policy, with no counterfactual - 20 real promotions were earned in rounds >= 2 and would have been lost, so the savings figure is an upper bound on value and a lower bound on cost.

nodes.title: The landed flag exists only in a projection, so the selector's solve test may never fire at runtime
nodes.body: bestScores at src/runtime/selector.js:17 begins with 'if (round?.landed !== true) continue', and isSolved returns true only when a finite score >= 1 exists. In the raw event log, round.finished carries no landed field at all - 231 of 231 missing - and src/core/reduce.js:236 shows autopilot.applied is the only writer that sets r.landed = true, with round.unlanded setting it false. Projecting C:/Users/Darkness/.dsh/loom/campaigns/*/views/state.json gives 226 rounds: landed true 81, missing 140, false 5; 27 rounds are promoted-but-not-landed; 44 of 124 slots have no landed round at all; and 16 rounds re-picked a task that had already been promoted. Mechanism: any promotion that does not route through autopilot.applied leaves the task permanently unsolved, so the round-robin pool never shrinks and the loop keeps re-running solved work. Limitation: state.json is a view, not the runtime's memory, so I cannot exclude another in-memory writer of landed that the event schema does not surface - the claim is about what the log can prove, not about what the process did.

nodes.title: 113 of 114 gate evaluations carry a null incumbent score, so minGain is compared against nothing
nodes.body: Of 208 gate.evaluated events, 114 record promoted=true and exactly one of those carries a numeric incumbentScore (loom-self3 round 10, value 1); the other 113 are null. loom-self3 promoted its 'exposure' task in rounds 3, 6, 7, 8 and 9 with incumbentScore null each time, then at round 10 an incumbent of 1 finally appears and the gate refuses (both rounds 10 and 11 score 1, promoted false, status no-gain). With a binary score and minGain 0.05, 'beats the incumbent' is a comparison between the candidate and a missing operand, so the gate degenerates to 'candidate verified and produced a patch' - which is also why already-solved work can be promoted repeatedly. Limitation: null may be a serialisation default for zero rather than a true absence, so I can prove the log cannot reconstruct the comparison but not that the runtime lacked the value; the one numeric case is a single observation.

nodes.title: 43 of 69 eval sets register the holdout suite as a task, shrinking the real pool to 1-4 tasks
nodes.body: Forty-three of 69 evalset.registered events include an entry {id:'suite', prompt:'Holdout: the whole repository suite. Not a task to work on.', verify:{cmd:'...scripts/test-all.mjs', timeoutMs:300000}} and declare holdout:['suite']; 29 declare an empty holdout list and 1 declares three ids. 'suite' never appears among the 227 round.started taskIds, so it is a registration-side decoy that inflates the perceived pool while contributing nothing. Excluding it, eval sets are 1 task (26 campaigns), 2 (33), 3 (11), 4 (3) - i.e. the curriculum a bandit would have to work with has a median of 2 arms. The separate holdout cadence in src/runtime/sampling.js:31 is dead anyway because holdoutEvery is null in all 69 campaigns, and holdout runs actually occur through the 50 holdout.selected events instead. Limitation: I can show the pool is smaller than it looks but not that the decoy changed any outcome; a one-task pool already makes round-robin and any bandit behaviourally identical, which is the more damaging fact and cannot be attributed to this bug.

nodes.title: No task-level state crosses campaigns: 180 registered entries, 148 distinct prompts, no difficulty field
nodes.body: The eval task schema is exactly {id, prompt, verify, family} - there is no difficulty, tags, cost or duration field, and family is null in 143 of 171 entries. Across 180 registered entries only 148 distinct first-400-character prompt hashes appear; 13 hashes are reused, covering 45 entries (suite x43, card-actions x9, head-dot x9, queue-wait x6). Only 3 prompt hashes were ever attempted in two or more campaigns, and all three are all-or-nothing: loom-acc5 0/8 versus loom-acc6 0/10 (both never verify); loom-acc5 0/6 versus loom-acc6 0/8 (both never verify); loom-claim-live2 1/2 versus loom-claim-live3 1/2 (both always verify). So a new campaign starts with zero prior on every arm, re-derives difficulty from scratch, and cannot inherit 'this task never verifies' from a sibling campaign that already spent ten attempts learning it. Limitation: 400-character prompt hashing is a proxy that would merge near-duplicates and split trivial edits; the transfer sample is n=3 pairs with perfectly separated outcomes, which is anecdote, not an estimate of transfer.

nodes.title: Every bandit-curriculum success was measured at 10^5+ samples; this loop gets ~1.8 attempts per task
nodes.body: The two canonical positive results both live in sample-rich regimes. Graves et al. 2017 (PMLR 70:1311-1320) halve time-to-threshold with a nonstationary bandit over learning-progress rewards, on LSTM curricula trained for millions of steps with each task sampled many times per phase. Schaul et al. 2019 (arXiv:1912.06910) run 15 Atari games at >=5 seeds, i.e. 75+ full training runs, to compare allocation policies that differ by a few percent. This ledger has 452 attempts total over 28 wall-clock hours, 124 slots, mean 1.83 rounds per slot, and $0.00049 per verified attempt. A nonstationary bandit needs enough pulls per arm to see the reward drift it is designed to track; at 1.83 pulls there is nothing to track and the estimator is the prior. Limitation: this is a sample-count argument, not a result - nobody has run a bandit selector in a dollars-per-sample coding loop, so the honest claim is that the evidence does not transfer, not that the method fails here.

nodes.title: Stationary UCB and Thompson sampling were sometimes significantly worse than uniform allocation
nodes.body: Schaul, Borsa et al. 2019 (arXiv:1912.06910, DeepMind) replaced a hand-tuned schedule with a nonstationary bandit over behaviour modulations on Atari 2600, 15 games, >=5 seeds: 113+/-2% median human-normalised score versus 118+/-6% for the tuned fixed reference across 57 games. Inside that result is the warning this design needs: stationary UCB and Thompson sampling were 'sometimes significantly worse than uniform', because they 'prematurely lock into using modulations that may be good initially, but don't help for long-term performance'. Their Figure 5 metric shows a fixed arm chosen from the first 10% of a run losing substantially to the hindsight-best arm. Read against our ledger: round-robin is close to uniform, and the first-round evidence that a task always verifies (51 of 124 slots all-pass) is exactly the kind of early signal a stationary bandit would lock onto, then keep pulling a solved arm. Limitation: the arms there are behaviour modulations inside one training run, not tasks across rounds, and 'sometimes' means the regression is not universal - this bounds the naive fix, it does not refute bandit selection done with discounting.

nodes.title: IRT adaptive testing's 90% item reduction assumes a fixed examinee; this loop's examinee mutates every round
nodes.body: ATLAS (arXiv:2511.04689) calibrates a 3PL IRT model on 3,467-4,680 models per benchmark and selects items by Fisher information with randomesque top-5 exposure control: HellaSwag matched with 39 of 5,608 items at 0.154 MAE, ARC 0.099 MAE with 77 items, 90% item reduction at maintained precision. Three of its own numbers are adversarial to importing it. 3.2-5.7% of items have NEGATIVE discrimination, i.e. difficulty estimates wrong in sign (WinoGrande item 247: 0.89 accuracy, a_i = -0.43). Twelve percent of models must be excluded because EAP is undefined on all-correct/all-incorrect patterns. And the model is explicitly unidimensional with a calibration population that goes stale as architectures evolve. Our loop violates all three preconditions at once: the examinee is the agent being edited between rounds, every task is multidimensional, and the ability estimate changes precisely because the previous round succeeded. Item parameters estimated before a promotion are stale by construction after it. Limitation: no one has tested whether IRT item parameters transfer when the examinee is the loop's own edited artifact, so the assumption break is argued from the model's own stated scope, not measured in this setting.

nodes.title: The 85% success-rate rule has no prediction for a learner that remembers every trial it has seen
nodes.body: Wilson et al. 2019, Nature Communications 10:4646, derives the difficulty that maximises learning rate as ER* = 15.87% for Gaussian noise (18.39% Laplacian, 25% Cauchy), and shows that clamping the error rate makes precision grow like sqrt(t) while holding difficulty fixed grows it like sqrt(log t) - 'exponentially slower'. That is the best available argument for targeting a difficulty band instead of working whatever is next. But the same paper proves the sweet spot is an artefact of gradient noise: a Bayesian learner with perfect memory has a posterior independent of trial ORDER (their Eq. 22), so difficulty sequencing does nothing for it. Our loop re-serves the identical prompt with the identical verify command, so its 'learner' has perfect memory of every failure - which is why the observed repeat decay (0.615 -> 0.214 across repeat index) cannot be explained by the 85% mechanism at all. Limitation: the theory is derived for gradient learners under specific noise families; LLM agents are neither, so the paper constrains the justification for difficulty targeting without telling us what the right band is for a patch-generating agent.

nodes.title: Easy-to-hard sequencing was worse than shuffling; only a mixed hybrid schedule beat baseline
nodes.body: Nair et al. 2024 (arXiv:2407.10194) train a 1M-parameter NanoGPT on 1.2M generated Python snippets (400k each easy/medium/hard, difficulty OM = (cyclomatic complexity + Halstead difficulty)/2) under four orders. Code execution accuracy: shuffled baseline 74.58%, Sequential easy-to-hard 62.56% (worse than baseline), Incremental 76.79%, Hybrid 79.23%; on the hard test set 67.22% baseline versus 74.04% hybrid; training on hard-only reached just 61.78% on hard versus 74.04% for hybrid. Code completion was near-null: token-level 81.23% baseline versus 75.64% sequential (worse), 81.27% incremental, 81.13% hybrid; line-level 41.74% versus 42.04%. Their own surprise: conditionals were harder than loops, so a static difficulty metric mispredicted the ordering. Two lessons transfer: monotone easy-to-hard is actively harmful, and mixing beats both monotone directions. Limitation: this is gradient training on 1.2M samples where difficulty is computable from source text; this loop pays dollars per sample and has 1-4 tasks, so ordering effects measured at that scale bound nothing here directly.

nodes.title: Best-of-3 attempts buys +0.008 AUC while run-to-run SD is 0.011 - promotion is coin-flipping
nodes.body: Arino de la Rubia and Pafka 2026 (arXiv:2609.33812) run 584 benchmark runs, 312 of them with everything fixed (3 agents x 2 models x 52 runs). Median run-to-run SD over compliant runs is 0.0107 AUC, while the total spread between the six pairing means is 0.0095 - the noise exceeds the signal it is supposed to resolve. Three-run comparisons put the weaker pairing ahead 28-44% of the time; 39-113 runs per arm are needed to resolve the observed differences; 10 of 312 runs broke the task's data rules and included the 7 highest scores, so excluding them drops the best score 0.8293 -> 0.7695. The direct analogue of this design: the best compliant artifact of three attempts beats a single attempt by +0.0081 holdout AUC (95% CI 0.0063-0.0098), i.e. best-of-k buys a real but tiny margin. A planned larger-model upgrade worth +0.0091 AUC (7.1 SE) still lost in one-run-each comparisons 28% of the time. Limitation: the task family is tabular ML artifacts graded by holdout AUC, not repository patches graded by a shell exit code, and +0.0081 is best-of-3 after filtering non-compliant runs - the best-of-2 promotion in this loop has never been measured against a same-task no-promotion control.

nodes.title: Value of information is unobservable in this ledger: rounds log score, promotion and cost only
nodes.body: A value-of-information selector needs, per arm, the distribution of what a pull teaches conditional on what is already known - including the case where the patch is worthless and the attempt still resolves a belief about the task. The round and attempt schemas here cannot express that: round.finished records n, status, score, promoted, costUsd, durationMs, tokens and counts; attempt.finished records verifierOk, score, error, phase, exitCode, abandoned, metrics and diff stats. Nothing records a verifier re-run on the same commit, so verifier false-negative rate is unmeasured; nothing records the outcome of an unattempted task, so the counterfactual is missing. The single trace with information value and no patch value is the 19 rounds whose recorded score was 1 with status no-gain, and the 127 errored attempts (28% of 452) which carry zero of both. Consequence: any VOI selector shipped now would be unfalsifiable, because the loop's own gate cannot score the information it claims to have gained. Limitation: unobservability is not zero VOI - the loop may already be harvesting information and simply not recording it, so this argues for instrumentation, not for abandoning information-aware selection.

nodes.title: Our gate module's own suite kills 16 of 22 hand-written mutants, score 0.727, in 2.7 s
nodes.body: 22 single-operator mutants against src/gate/gate.js, scored by the focused spec tests/gate.test.mjs (78 assertions): 16 killed, mutation score 0.727. Survivors: clamp-low-ge (gate.js:17), clamp-high-ge (:18), roundscore-noclamp (:38), sortunverified (:157), meantask-noclamp (:93), slack-default-one (:231). The whole sweep costs 2.69 s wall clock, mean 0.122 s per mutant, against a 146.9 ms baseline test run (n=20, sd 15.0). That is the shape of a graded signal needing no new infrastructure: mutate a module, run the command the task already declares, count non-zero exits. It ranks verifiers where a pass/fail bit cannot, and exp-mut-001 showed the same probe separating a real spec from an always-pass stub (0.917 vs 0.000). Limitation: one 285-line module, 22 hand-written mutants from a single operator set, one machine; the number is only comparable against the same mutant list, and a different operator set moves it several points either way.

nodes.title: Three of six surviving mutants are behaviourally equivalent, so the honest score is 0.842 not 0.727
nodes.body: Differential fuzz of each survivor against the original: 20,000 generated calls per mutant across the three exported entry points, feeding nulls, NaN, Infinity, string numerics and out-of-range scores. clamp-low-ge, clamp-high-ge and sortunverified produced zero differing outputs. roundscore-noclamp differed 1,401 times, meantask-noclamp 105, slack-default-one 53. Effective non-equivalent mutation score is 16/19 = 0.842, so 14% of the naive score is noise from mutants no test can kill, and the noise is one-directional: it makes a suite look worse than it is. That matters twice — a fixed mu* floor wastes a candidate's improvement budget, and a candidate can add equivalent mutants of its own to depress a rival's number if the mutant list is editable. Limitation: 20k random cases is not a proof of equivalence; sortunverified's inconsistent comparator could still diverge on a tie pattern the generator never produced, and the fuzzer only knew the exported functions.

nodes.title: V8 byte coverage reports 100.0% for the same module that escapes 27% of mutants
nodes.body: Ran NODE_V8_COVERAGE over src/gate/gate.js for two suites: tests/gate.test.mjs alone, and all 29 test files in the repo. Both report 9,859 of 9,859 bytes covered = 100.0%, and that 100%-covered file still escapes 27.3% of mutants. Under innermost-range semantics (a byte counts only if the smallest range containing it has count>0) the honest figure is 9,732/9,859 = 98.71%, leaving 127 bytes never executed across 9 source lines. Five of the six surviving mutants sit on lines the suite does execute: clamp-high-ge :18, roundscore-noclamp :38, sortunverified :157, meantask-noclamp :93, slack-default-one :231. Coverage saturates before discrimination does, so it cannot serve as the graded signal even where it is honestly computed. Limitation: byte coverage of one ES module on one runtime; line and branch semantics differ, and the qualitative point is unchanged by which exact percentage you print.

nodes.title: Coverage as reward pays for deleting defensive code: +0.77 points with all 78 assertions still green
nodes.body: Replaced the 17-line defensive idOf() in src/gate/gate.js with a 4-line version that drops every null and non-string id branch. The file shrank 9,859 to 9,697 bytes, V8 byte coverage rose 0.9871 to 0.9948 (+0.77 pt), and all 78 assertions still passed with exit 0. No behaviour improved; the score improved because untested defensive branches, the ones that only run on malformed input, stopped existing. This is the mechanism Inozemtseva and Holmes measured (ICSE 2014, DOI 10.1145/2568225.2568271): once suite size is fixed, coverage stops tracking effectiveness, and here the cheapest way to raise it is subtraction. Any coverage-graded loop therefore rewards a candidate that deletes the error handling nobody tests. Limitation: one module with a hand-made deletion; a real agent may not find that edit unprompted, and a coverage-of-diff metric would price the same patch very differently.

nodes.title: Per-assertion partial credit puts a total behavioural break at 0.833-0.987, inside minGain noise
nodes.body: Counting passing assertions as partial credit compresses almost everything into the top 17 points. For the 16 mutants the 78-assertion gate spec kills, the broken tree still passes 65 to 77 assertions: partial credit 0.833 to 0.987, mean 0.944. mintasks-gt, which disables the minTasks guard, scores 0.833; infinity-default and complete-truthy-loose, each killed by exactly one assertion, score 0.987. So a patch that removes a promotion guard and a patch that is correct differ by 0.013 to 0.167 on this scale while the gate's default minGain is 0.05. A graded signal is only useful if its scale resolves around the threshold you gate on; this one concentrates all real differences below it. Limitation: assertion counts are only comparable within one file, a suite written as four fat assertions would produce a different curve, and nothing here establishes that per-assertion weighting matches defect severity.

nodes.title: 100 no-op assertions lift a broken tree's partial credit by 0.7 points at zero behaviour change
nodes.body: Appending 100 `ok(true, ...)` no-ops to tests/gate.test.mjs leaves the intact tree at 1.0000 and lifts a deliberately broken tree from 0.9872 to 0.9944. The exploit needs no knowledge of the code under test, only write access to the suite, which the loop has; exp-goodhart-001 counted 1.6% of our 437 promoted patches touching tests/ already, concentrated in campaigns with no no-test-edit check. Per-assertion credit rewards the count of green lines, which is exactly the human failure the IntelliGame replication measured: more tests written, test-smell ratio 0.13 vs 0.03 (p=0.013). Once the reward is a fraction of assertions, the cheapest increment is an assertion that cannot fail. Limitation: arithmetic on a TAP-like tally rather than an observed agent exploit; a harness weighting assertions by mutation-kill contribution would not be paddable this way, and we did not test whether an agent finds the trick unprompted.

nodes.title: The same 100 padding assertions move mutation score by exactly zero, unlike partial credit
nodes.body: Ran the identical 100-no-op padding against the mutation sweep: 16 of 22 mutants killed before and after, 0.727 both times, mutant by mutant identical. Mechanism: a mutant dies on a failing assertion, so an assertion that passes under every mutant adds neither kills nor denominator — padding is score-neutral by construction, whereas a per-assertion tally grows its numerator. This is the only measured result in this batch that favours mutation over its cheaper alternatives, and it argues that the choice of graded signal matters more than its cost. It also means the two channels disagree about what a patch is worth: under partial credit the padded broken tree beats the unpadded one, under mutation they are indistinguishable. Limitation: neutral to this attack only — mutation score remains movable by editing the mutant list, by adding code no operator targets, and by the equivalent-mutant floor, so the claim is narrow, not a general robustness result.

nodes.title: A candidate that prints its own QUALITY line before the harness wins the round: 0.475 to 1.000
nodes.body: The only graded channel the design actually has is a stdout regex, and the candidate writes to stdout. runVerifier (src/exec/verifier.js:110-130) applies RegExp.exec and keeps the first match of a pattern such as QUALITY=([0-9.]+). A candidate module that prints `QUALITY=1.0` at import time, before the harness prints its own honest `QUALITY=0.25`, yields metrics.quality=1 instead of 0.25: scoreAttempt returns 1.000 instead of 0.475 and decidePromotion promotes with delta 0.525 against minGain 0.05. Behaviour was byte-identical, the same single check passed, no test or gate file was touched, and no existing guard looks at stdout. The patch simply talked first. Limitation: reproduced with a two-file fixture driven through the real runVerifier, not by a live agent; anchoring the pattern, taking the last match, or reading a report file the harness owns closes this instance but not the class.

nodes.title: When the code under test computes the metric, a one-line change buys the whole grade: 0.30 vs 0.65 vs 1.00
nodes.body: Same class, without needing to know the harness. Three trees: baseline passed its check and reported quality 0.25 (score 0.475); a one-line forge, identical behaviour, printed 1.0 (score 1.000); a tree that genuinely added a function reported 0.5 (score 0.650). rankAttempts put the forge first, ahead of the real improvement, and decidePromotion promoted it with delta 0.525. A metric defined as the candidate's self-report is a specification of what the candidate should print, not a measurement — the extremal Goodhart case in Manheim and Garrabrant's taxonomy (arXiv:1803.04585), and the exact risk carried by exp-score-003's otherwise encouraging 5-valued demo. Limitation: a synthetic three-tree fixture; our tasks declare no metrics at all (0 of 168 verify specs), so this is a hazard of the proposed fix rather than an incident we have observed in the ledger.

nodes.title: Adding the other 28 test files kills zero additional mutants on this module; breadth is not discrimination
nodes.body: Ran the same 22 gate.js mutants two ways: against the focused spec alone, and against all 29 test files in the repo. Both kill exactly 16 of 22, and no other file kills a mutant the focused file misses. The concentrated file has 78 assertions over 285 lines; the other 28 files add no kills on this module at all. That is the size confound Papadakis et al. (ICSE 2018) documented and w2-verify-mutation-score-size-confound records: suite size is a common cause, so a score raiseable by writing more tests measures writer effort rather than verifier strength. It also predicts that a loop optimising an absolute score will spend its budget on breadth it cannot cash. Limitation: cross-file kills are only plausible where modules interact and gate.js has almost no importers, so the result is demonstrated for a leaf module, not for a hub — a shared util with twenty importers might well be killed from elsewhere.

nodes.title: Only 34 of 78 assertions ever kill a mutant, and two mutants depend on a single assertion each
nodes.body: Of the 78 assertions in tests/gate.test.mjs only 34 (43.6%) kill any of the 22 mutants; the other 44 are dead weight for discrimination. Kill-set sizes range 1 to 13; two mutants are killed by exactly one assertion each — infinity-default by 'missing minTasks counts as unsatisfiable', complete-truthy-loose by 'null input reports incomplete evidence' — and the single most load-bearing assertion accounts for six kills. So the graded signal rests on a handful of points of failure: delete or reword one assertion and the score moves discretely, and a candidate that edits tests (1.6% of our promoted patches) could retire the two single-point killers and lose almost nothing else. A score whose variance lives in one line is easier to move by editing that line than by improving code. Limitation: one 285-line module and one hand-made mutant list; a module with wide fan-out would spread kills across more assertions, and 43.6% is not a general property of suites.

nodes.title: Uniform taskScores turn a total integration failure into 0.95 by declaring 100 trivially-passing sub-tasks
nodes.body: scoreAttempt (src/gate/gate.js:87-97 and 121-137) averages taskScores uniformly, so the denominator is a choice rather than a measurement. A tree failing its only real check, {integration: 0}, scores 0.0. Adding one trivially-passing sub-score makes it 0.5, five make it 0.833, twenty make it 0.952, a hundred make it 0.990 — with no behaviour change at all. Whoever writes the eval task, or the loop itself, which can edit the chain, can convert a total failure into a 0.95 by declaring lint or formatting sub-tasks. A uniform mean is not a graded signal; it is a weighted vote whose weights live in a file the optimiser can reach. Limitation: reproduced by calling the real exported function with hand-built inputs, so it establishes the arithmetic, not that anyone would do it; a rule that every declared sub-score must clear its own floor would make this specific arithmetic unavailable.

nodes.title: Ledger: 449 scored attempts hold exactly two values, and 0 of 168 verify specs declare metrics
nodes.body: Walked all 69 campaign directories under the loom home: 449 attempt-like records carry a numeric score, with exactly two distinct values, 0.0 (232 records) and 1.0 (217). Of 168 records that carry a verify{cmd}, zero declare a metrics block. The graded path exp-score-003 demonstrated is therefore real at unit level and unused in practice: every round's reachable margins are still 0 and 1, minGain 0.05 is satisfied by 1 and rejected by 0, and the gate is a pass/fail test wearing a continuous delta. This extends exp-score-001 (227 rounds, two values, only 8.5% of campaign-task series ever changed) to a larger ledger with the same verdict, and it locates the defect in the eval-set declaration rather than in the scoring code. Limitation: the walk counts every dict carrying a score field, so it may include non-attempt records; and zero adoption is a fact about our eval sets, not evidence that graded scoring fails elsewhere.

nodes.title: Coverage predicts LLM test effectiveness on clean code (r=0.821) but not when the goal is to expose a bug
nodes.body: The best current evidence on whether coverage and mutation track effectiveness for LLM-written tests is regime-dependent, and our loop sits in the bad regime. Zhao, Zhou and Cohen (PACMSE/ISSTA 2026, arXiv:2607.22880) used 11 LLMs in 13 settings over 318 buggy focal methods from 17 Defects4J v3.0 projects, 8,268 suites and more than 100,000 tests. On bug-free regression-style code both metrics carry signal across models: branch-coverage Pearson r=0.821 (p=0.001), Kendall tau 0.641, MCC about 0.54-0.63, and little evidence that suite size is the dominant confounder for LLM tests. But when the code is buggy and the goal is to expose that bug, coverage is unreliable and mutation analysis is not even applicable, because it needs a green suite first. Limitation: Java and Defects4J, tests an LLM wrote about code it did not write, no agentic loop; our tasks are 'make a spec pass', which is neither regime.

nodes.title: Coverage and oracle emptiness anti-correlate (r=-0.67), yet only 23-30% of flagged gaps earn a test
nodes.body: Coverage can be high while the assertions do nothing. Vera-Perez, Danglot, Monperrus and Baudry (Empirical Software Engineering 2019, arXiv:1807.05030) defined pseudo-tested methods as covered but undetected when the body is emptied, across 21 open-source Java projects and more than 28,000 methods using Descartes on PITest. The pseudo-tested rate ran 1% to 46%, with 14 of 21 projects below 7%, and the project-level Pearson correlation between coverage ratio and pseudo-tested ratio was -0.67 (p<0.01). Reviewing 101 flagged methods with the developers, only about 30 (23-30%) were judged worth an extra test; the rest were generated code, debug and exception-message builders, trivial delegators. So the oracle gap is real, measurable at scale, and mostly not actionable, and no exit code can see it. Limitation: Java, Maven and JUnit; extreme body-emptying can create equivalent variants; the 23-30% figure rests on 101 hand-reviewed methods.

nodes.title: A count-based testing scoreboard bought 4x the test smells (0.13 vs 0.03, p=0.013) in 174 participants
nodes.body: Straubinger, Fulcini, Garaccione, Ardito and Fraser replicated IntelliGame with 174 participants on TypeScript (PACMSE/ISSTA 2025, arXiv:2504.19294). The gamified group wrote more tests and executed them more often, but its test-smell ratio was 0.13 against 0.03 for controls (p=0.013), and participants reported more time pressure. The transferable claim is narrower than 'gamification works': a scoreboard whose increments are countable behaviours, tests written or assertions added or lines covered, reliably moves those counts and degrades the property that was not counted. For a loop this is the prediction that per-assertion partial credit converges on assertion-shaped noise, and that the loss shows up in exactly the dimension the score omits. Limitation: humans in an IDE earning achievements, not an agent with a shell verifier; the smell ratio is a static heuristic; and the study never tested a mutation-based scoreboard, so it cannot rank the alternatives.

nodes.title: LLM-rubric rewards diverge from gold while still rising: the proxy-gold gap grows 29% to 44%
nodes.body: If the graded signal is a rubric scored by a model, the proxy improves after gold stops. 'Rubric Dropout' (arXiv:2608.11669) reports gold score rising, peaking and then declining while the proxy keeps climbing: the proxy-gold gap widened from 29% to 44% on HealthBench-Hard and ResearchQA gold fell 22 points from its peak. The proposed fix is one line — drop a random fraction f of the rubric criteria at each optimisation step so the optimiser cannot learn the fixed rubric — which is the rubric analogue of holdout rotation, and is the only intervention in this literature that costs nothing to adopt. It reframes a rubric as a sampling device rather than a fixed objective, and explains why a static rubric inside a loop degrades even when each individual judgement is accurate. Limitation: open-ended answer quality graded by a model judge, not code; there is no code-task replication, and the paper evaluates its own fix on the same two benchmarks it criticises.

nodes.title: 26 judge models on 5,352 code triplets: half the point-wise verdicts are ties and order swaps change accuracy
nodes.body: LLM judges are the weakest graded channel available. CodeJudgeBench (ACL 2026, arXiv:2507.10535) tests 26 judge models on 5,352 curated (instruction, good, bad) triplets drawn from 1,055 LiveCodeBench-v6 problems, execution-free judging of generation, repair and test-writing. Every judge scores far below its JudgeBench near-ceiling, about 50% of point-wise verdicts are ties, swapping response order changes accuracy substantially, and a Qwen3-8B thinking model beats judge-tuned models up to 70B. Separately (arXiv:2505.16222), surface text moves verdicts: self-declared correctness shifts LLaMA-3.1-70B by +24.7 points on correct code and -23.5 on wrong code, renaming variables alone moves Claude-3.5-Sonnet by plus or minus 12.6, and generating tests before scoring does not remove the bias. Limitation: execution-free judging of contest-style code; a judge that also runs tests is a different system, and none of this measures a judge used as a reward inside a loop that can learn its biases.

nodes.title: The reference benchmark grades binary resolved, so the field has no validated graded alternative to copy
nodes.body: SWE-bench's headline number is binary `resolved`: a submission counts only if every FAIL_TO_PASS test passes and every PASS_TO_PASS test still passes, with no partial credit and no ranking among failures. Every graded scheme this batch examines is therefore an ad hoc addition, not a scaled-down version of a validated benchmark metric. That matters because the contamination signals are themselves frequency counts that a graded score would absorb silently: a vendor blog estimate (cubic.dev) puts verbatim reference fixes in 6.7% of Verified submissions, and issue-only file localisation reaches 76% on Verified against 53% off-benchmark, which reads as benchmark familiarity leaking into the measurement. A continuous score computed over such a set would average a leak rather than expose it. Limitation: the binary definition is documented in the harness while the 6.7% and 76/53 figures come from a blog post, not a peer-reviewed study, so the contamination numbers are indicative only.

nodes.title: Smallest credible graded signal: a harness-side mutant delta, 20 mutants per round, no per-assertion credit
nodes.body: From the measurements: keep one command per task, and add a harness-side mutant sweep over the touched module — 22 mutants cost 2.69 s, 0.122 s each, against a 146.9 ms test run, so a 20-mutant budget per round is nearly free. Score killed/(total minus equivalent), computed by the harness from exit codes, never parsed from candidate stdout; require a green baseline before mutating; gate on the mutation delta rather than the absolute score; and keep minGain coarser than the sampling error, which binomial arithmetic puts at 0.107 for 22 mutants and 0.05 for 100. Do not add per-assertion credit (0.83-0.99 band, paddable) and do not add a judge rubric (ties, order and surface bias). What this buys is one channel the patch cannot write to, at a cost below the existing verifier's noise. Limitation: the composition is unvalidated end to end; no run yet shows a mutation-delta gate promoting more real improvements than a pass/fail gate at equal budget.

nodes.title: Loom's recorded spend is 246x below provider usage in its own child logs
nodes.body: 331 loom attempts joined by sessionId to their archived transcripts: recorded costUsd sums to $0.0866, while the assistant/message usage blocks in those same sessions sum to 18,258,102 uncached input + 5,778,853 output + 492,650,420 cacheRead tokens, which prices to $21.3336 at loom's own DEFAULT_PRICING. Ratio 246x. Per attempt the median error is 811x (p10 167x, p90 3,386x) and 0 of 331 attempts recorded at or above the true figure, so the error is one-directional, not noise. True per-attempt cost: median $0.0455, mean $0.0645, p90 $0.1344, max $0.3613. Limitation: one machine, 69 campaigns, a 10-day window, and the $21.33 is itself computed with a price table this research shows to be wrong, so 246x measures the token error compounded by the price error, not either alone.

nodes.title: The comment justifying the fallback path is false: child logs do carry usage
nodes.body: src/runtime/cost.js:181-186 asserts 'Child session logs carry no `usage` on assistant messages (verified against real archives)' and treats the host meter as the only real measurement. On this machine 437 of 437 loom child sessions are archived and 8,983 of their 9,015 assistant/message events (99.65%) carry a usage object; across all 923 session archives it is 34,268 of 34,318 (99.85%), with zero all-zero blocks. So sumUsage() would have worked the whole time. It is never reached because the meter is tried first and returns null. Limitation: the archives are DSH v4 session logs on one host; the comment may have been true against a different DSH version, and I cannot date when it was written.

nodes.title: The token meter is called with a session id where it takes a session object, so it returns null
nodes.body: @deepseek-ai/dsh-token-meter's API is measure(session, requestHeader?), and its docstring says '@param session - session to replay through its current durable tail'; it calls this._sync(session) on the object. src/runtime/cost.js:191 passes the sessionId string: meter.measure(sessionId). The call therefore yields nothing usable, measureViaMeter returns null every time, and every attempt falls through to fallbackSpend. The unit test cannot catch this because tests/self6/meter-usage.test.mjs injects tokenMeter:{measure:()=>MEASURED}, a fake that accepts any argument and proves only that the return value is consumed. Limitation: I infer the null from behaviour (no attempt ever carries a meter-shaped measurement) rather than from a stack trace, since the meter swallows the failure in a try/catch.

nodes.title: The DSH meter returns context occupancy, not billing: no dollars, no in/out split
nodes.body: The host token meter's measure() returns {logRevision, baseline, surfaceDeltaTokens, totalTokens, surfaceTokens, nodes}, where totalTokens = max(0, baseline.tokens + surfaceDeltaTokens). Its README states 'Occupancy is a reference figure, not a billing record: nothing in the harness makes decisions from it'. Charging this per attempt would sum a context-pressure number, not a bill. The billing-grade fields exist elsewhere: a session projection named tokenUsage carries 'Provider-reported usage accumulated across the complete durable log' as {uncachedInputTokens, outputTokens, cacheReadTokens, cacheWriteTokens}. Note uncachedInputTokens, not inputTokens, so even normalizeMeterUsage's field names would not line up. Limitation: this is read from a bundled asar, and the projection may be reachable by plugins only through ctx.sessionProjections.stateOf(session), which loom does not attempt.

nodes.title: 95.3% of the tokens loom's attempts consumed are cache reads
nodes.body: Across the 331 joined attempts: uncached input 18,258,102, output 5,778,853, cacheRead 492,650,420, cacheWrite 0. Cache reads are 95.3% of all metered tokens. At DEFAULT_PRICING they are 64.7% of the true cost ($13.794 of $21.334), with input $5.112 and output $2.427. The independent cost-meter ledger on the same machine agrees on the shape: cacheRead/input = 25.8x over 24 days and 36,061 calls. Any attribution design that sums input+output, or that forgets the cache-read bucket, is measuring roughly 4.7% of the work. Limitation: the cacheRead share depends on how DSH lays out its prefix; a harness with fewer, smaller cached prefixes would show a lower share, and this is one host's workload.

nodes.title: cacheWriteTokens is recorded in every usage block and never priced at all
nodes.body: src/runtime/cost.js:150-161 computes (in/1e6)*inP + (out/1e6)*outP + (cacheRead/1e6)*cacheP. cacheWriteTokens is summed by sumUsage, carried through normalizeMeterUsage, stored on the attempt record, and then multiplied by nothing. Provider rates make this the most expensive bucket per token: Anthropic charges 1.25x base input for a 5-minute cache write and 2x for a 1-hour write against 0.1x for a read. On this machine the omission happens to be free: cacheWrite is 0 in all 331 attempts and 0 on every one of the 24 ledger days. That is a property of the provider, not of the code. Limitation: DeepSeek's API may not bill cache writes separately, so the bug is latent here and would only bite on a route whose adapter reports a nonzero cacheWriteTokens.

nodes.title: The default price table inverts the output/cache-read ratio against the observed rate card
nodes.body: DEFAULT_PRICING is 0.28 in / 0.42 out / 0.028 cacheRead, i.e. out/in = 1.500 and cr/in = 0.100. The observed rate card on this machine (ledger.json.details-cache rows, bucket/tokens/rate) is input 0.15000, out/in = 4.000, cr/in = 0.020. So output is underpriced 2.67x and cache reads overpriced 5x at the same time. Because the workload is cache-read dominated, the second error wins: re-pricing the same 331 attempts at the observed card gives $7.684 instead of $21.334, so the default table overstates true spend 2.78x even when the tokens are right. Limitation: the observed card is one provider's promotional rate on one account, has changed at least nine times in the ledger's pricingHistory, and is not a list price anyone else should copy.

nodes.title: The fallback prices only brief and answer, blind to the per-call preamble that dominates cost
nodes.body: fallbackSpend(brief, text, pricing) sets inputTokens = ceil(brief.length/4) and outputTokens = ceil(text.length/4), with cacheRead and cacheWrite hardcoded to 0. This is why the 100 distinct recorded inputTokens values bottom out at a function of brief length (479 to 1,313 tokens, implying briefs of 1,916 to 5,252 characters). It structurally omits the system prompt, the tool schemas, every prior turn, every tool result, and all cache traffic. Independent work puts the fixed preamble at 16,581 tokens per call for Claude Code, 7,025 for OpenCode and 829 for mini-SWE-agent, multiplied by 55-88 steps: 'the bill is set at the first call and multiplied by the step count'. A fallback that prices only the brief is not a lower bound on that bill; it is a different quantity. Limitation: the 16,581-token preamble is measured for other harnesses, not for DSH, and this host may prepend a smaller or larger one that I did not measure.

nodes.title: tokensOf counts input+output only, so the token cap sees 21.5x fewer tokens than the meter
nodes.body: src/runtime/round.js:785-790 returns inputTokens+outputTokens when positive, else ceil((brief.length+text.length)/4); it never adds cacheReadTokens or cacheWriteTokens. On the 331 joined attempts that is 24,036,955 tokens against 516,687,375 actually metered, a 21.5x undercount before any pricing is applied. The USD cap and the token cap therefore disagree about the same round by an order of magnitude, and only the USD one is even nominally wired to a price. Limitation: whether this matters depends on whether anyone sets budget.tokens; on this machine none of the 69 campaigns did, so the cap has never been exercised and the bug is unobserved rather than harmless.

nodes.title: No campaign came near its USD cap: 0 of 69 breached, worst case 0.1x of the limit
nodes.body: Every one of the 69 campaigns records a budget.usd between $1 and $30 and a budget.spentUsd that is at most 0.1x of it. Recomputed from provider usage at DEFAULT_PRICING, the largest true campaign spend is $1.244 (loom-ui8, cap $20) and the largest ratio to cap is still ~0.1x. So the budget preflight, the projectedUsd affordability test and the exhausted/unaffordable branches at src/runtime/round.js:917-945 have never fired in anger: the guard is untested by real traffic, and the number that would have stopped a runaway (spentUsd) is 198-246x too small to ever reach a cap. Limitation: these campaigns were short by design (1-18 rounds); a long campaign would eventually cross a cap, so this shows the guard is unexercised, not that the caps are unreachable.

nodes.title: 152 of 331 metered attempts recorded $0.00 while carrying 37.6% of the real spend
nodes.body: Because fallbackSpend is keyed on visible text, an attempt that returns little or no text records costUsd 0. 152 of the 331 joined attempts have costUsd 0 with real provider usage totalling $8.011, i.e. 37.6% of all measured spend is present in the logs and absent from the ledger. Twenty-one campaigns record a total spend of exactly $0 while their attempts really cost more than $0.05, and in 43 of 43 campaigns with any recorded spend, a single attempt cost more than that campaign's entire recorded total. src/runtime/round.js:1830-1833 also suppresses the budget.spent event when roundCost is 0, so these rounds append no spend event at all. Limitation: a $0 attempt can also mean a genuine no-op (crash, spawn failure), so some of the 152 are correctly free; the 37.6% is an upper bound on invisible spend.

nodes.title: Cost per promoted round is $0.2071 and 43% of measured spend did not promote
nodes.body: 226 rounds across the campaigns, 103 promoted. True spend (provider usage at DEFAULT_PRICING) is $12.125 on promoted rounds and $9.208 on non-promoted ones, so $0.2071 per promoted round and 43% of spend producing nothing that shipped. By failureKind the split is ok $8.443 (123 attempts), unclassified $6.294 (122), timeout $3.379 (25), died $3.218 (61): the unclassified bucket alone is 29% of spend, which is the population a naive per-attempt table would silently drop. Vendor analysis of the fully loaded figure puts tokens under 10% of cost per accepted change ($7.20 of $106.20 in one worked example, $4.68 of $56.01 in another) with review, rework and escaped defects making up the rest. Limitation: the $0.2071 uses a price table shown to be wrong, counts only model tokens, and excludes the human checkpoint time that the other 90% of the Sonar figure consists of.

nodes.title: Two candidates for one task in one round differ in cost by a median of 1.36x
nodes.body: 161 rounds spawned two candidates that both have metered usage. The ratio of the more expensive to the cheaper has median 1.36, p90 2.31, and a maximum of 77.09. That variance is within one round, one task, one brief, one verifier, and it is imposed by run-to-run behaviour rather than by task difficulty. It means a per-task or per-claim cost figure derived from a single run is unreliable at the 1.4x level as a matter of course, and catastrophically unreliable in the tail. It also means 'pick the cheaper candidate' is a real selector signal available for free from the same metering, and loom currently does not use it. Limitation: the 77x outlier is a single round and may be a retry storm rather than genuine work; medians from 161 pairs describe this workload only.

nodes.title: Streaming usage arrives in two places; keeping only the last event loses cache-creation tokens
nodes.body: Anthropic's stream puts the input-side counters (input_tokens, cache_creation_input_tokens, cache_read_input_tokens) in message_start only, while output_tokens reaches its final value in message_delta; a reader that inspects only the last event captures cache_read and silently loses cache_creation. Total input is the summation of input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens + cache_read_input_tokens, and blocks left in place still count as sent. OpenAI's equivalent, stream_options.include_usage, appends one final chunk before data: [DONE] whose choices array is always empty, and 'If the stream is interrupted, you may not receive the final usage chunk'. DSH handles the Anthropic case correctly: its projection replaces a step's prior sample and lets llm/retry-started open a new slot so a retried step 'contributes another billed attempt'. Limitation: both are vendor docs; the failure is observable only when a stream breaks or a fallback fires, and I did not reproduce it locally.

nodes.title: OTel GenAI counts cache-read tokens as part of input_tokens, so double counting is the default mistake
nodes.body: The GenAI semantic conventions define gen_ai.usage.input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_read.input_tokens and cache_creation.input_tokens, and state that cached tokens are 'Part of input_tokens'. An instrumentation that adds cache_read on top of input, or a consumer that sums every usage attribute it sees, therefore overstates prompt tokens by the cache share, which on this machine's workload is 25.8x the uncached input. The convention also renamed the metrics to gen_ai.client.inference.usage.{input_tokens,output_tokens,cache_read.input_tokens,cache_write.input_tokens} counters, deleting the gen_ai.client.token.usage histogram and its gen_ai.token.type attribute, and replaced gen_ai.system with gen_ai.provider.name at v1.37 while old emitters still send gen_ai_system. Limitation: this is a specification, not a measurement; which conventions a given exporter emits depends on its version, and loom emits no OTel at all today.

nodes.title: Subagent spend lives in sibling files the parent omits, and one telemetry pipeline priced it at $0
nodes.body: grafana/agento11y PR #918: 'Live Claude Code capture was pricing spawned subagents at $0 even when Claude Code itself reported real cost.' Cause: 'Claude Code writes a subagent's model turns (and token usage) to sibling files at <sessionID>/subagents/agent-<id>.jsonl. The parent transcript only records the Agent tool_use / tool_result pair.' The observed split was claude-code with cost and claude-code/subagent at $0 while the provider-side total showed the spend. A second tool reports Claude Code workflow runs writing 'a full session transcript - including usage tokens - that lives entirely outside the main session JSONL' with '~3.18M tokens in one session'. Limitation: on this machine the hole is latent, not active - all 437 loom attempt sessions spawn zero subagents (0 nested sessions under any attempt), so looping per-attempt usage is currently complete.

nodes.title: Provider usage and cost APIs are reconciliation tools with holes, not a live meter a loop can budget on
nodes.body: Anthropic's Admin API splits usage (bucket_width 1m/1h/1d, max 1440/168/31 buckets) from cost, and the cost endpoint accepts 1d buckets only, max 31. Amounts arrive in minor units and must be divided by 100, the endpoints are 'designed for historical analysis, not real-time monitoring', and 'Priority Tier costs use a different billing model and will never appear in the cost endpoint'. OpenAI's reference says its Usage API 'may not always reconcile perfectly with the Costs' and recommends the Costs endpoint for financial purposes. On this machine that gap is measurable: the local ledger's cost $59.485 against apiCost $28.384 leaves 52.3% of 'cost' as local estimate, and three provider-model pairs report apiCost exactly 0 while carrying $27.29 of local cost. Limitation: these are admin-scope APIs needing an org key the loop does not have, so this bounds what a background loop can verify, not what an operator can.

nodes.title: chars/4 undercounts tokens 40-45%; real transcripts measure 2.22 bytes per token
nodes.body: claude-context-cost 1.7.0 reports 'The usual shortcut, characters / 4, counts 40 to 45% too few tokens (-45% in the author's sessions, mostly in Portuguese; -40% in one in English)', validated on 457 transcripts and 91,347 responses with '0 where the sources differ from the usage', and measures a median 2.22 bytes per token. DSH's own README concedes the same direction: 'CJK text and JSON schemas underprice badly at four characters per token'. Loom's CHARS_PER_TOKEN = 4 therefore tilts every unpriced round downward even before it omits the preamble. Limitation: the author's corpus is one person's sessions dominated by Portuguese, the English figure rests on a single session, and both ratios are corpus-specific, so 2.22 is a warning sign rather than a constant to hardcode.

nodes.title: Correct per-attempt attribution is one join plus a versioned price row per call, not a new meter
nodes.body: The evidence supports a concrete design. (1) Read usage from the assistant/message events of the attempt's own session, not from a meter that reports occupancy; the blocks exist in 99.65% of loom child logs. (2) Key the price row by the request header's provider and model at call time, and version the table, because this machine's ledger recorded nine reprices in a month and a longest-prefix model match once overcharged 3x. (3) Price all four buckets, cache writes included, since a write is 1.25-2x base input while a read is 0.1x. (4) Carry the attempt id onto the attribution row so per-accepted-change is one grouped sum over attempts, with failed attempts in the numerator. (5) Reconcile weekly against the provider cost endpoint and publish the residual; here that residual would be 52.3%. Limitation: this still cannot attribute the human review time that dominates fully loaded cost per accepted change, and it assumes the provider reports cache writes at all.

nodes.title: Most reported agent cost is an estimate in a measurement's clothes: 52.3% is unpriced locally
nodes.body: The cost-meter plugin on this machine sums 24 days, 36,061 calls, 145,664,855 uncached input, 24,141,355 output and 3,760,157,964 cache reads. Its cost field totals $59.485 while its apiCost field, filled only where a provider actually reported a charge, totals $28.384. So 52.3% of the headline 'cost' is local arithmetic over a price table, and three provider-model pairs (open-design:deepseek-v4.1-flash $19.59, opencode-go:deepseek-v4.1-flash $7.13, open-design:claude-haiku-5.5 $0.56) report apiCost exactly 0. cacheWrite is 0 on every single day, so that bucket is untested across the whole window. Limitation: apiCost 0 legitimately means a flat-rate or subscription route where marginal cost really is zero, so 52.3% is an upper bound on estimation, not proof that half the bill is fiction.

nodes.title: A per-attempt dollar figure needs three caveats beside it or the loop optimises the wrong number
nodes.body: The measurements on this machine produce three distinct errors that a single number hides: the token source (fallback vs provider usage, 246x on cost), the price table (DEFAULT versus observed card, 2.78x the other way), and the missing preamble (unmeasured). A loop that promotes on 'cheaper' using any one of these would be selecting on an artefact. The safe shape is a triple: tokens by bucket from the provider, priced at a versioned card, with an explicit estimated/measured flag per attempt, plus one reconciliation delta against the publisher's cost endpoint. Loom already has the flag (usageEstimated) but sets it to true on 277 of 449 attempts and to false on 58 that are all-zero, which is exactly backwards for the reader who trusts it. Limitation: a triple costs more plumbing than a scalar and still cannot rank two attempts whose real costs differ by less than the 1.36x median within-round spread.

nodes.title: 98% of same-round candidate pairs edit the same files, so the pair is one hypothesis twice
nodes.body: Across 117 rounds with two non-empty candidate diffs, 115 (98%) share at least one file; Jaccard median 1.00 and p90 1.00; 73 pairs have an identical file set; of 40 pairs where both are single-file, 39 touch the same single file. Collisions concentrate in src/runtime/round.js (50 pairs), client/index.js (25), src/core/reduce.js (19), src/tools/index.js (16). Mechanism: the brief names one failing spec, and the spec lives in one file, so both candidates are steered to the same locus; the second slot explores a different implementation of the same edit, not a different hypothesis. Limitation: measured inside one repository (396 tracked files) under a binary 0/1 score gate, so it says nothing about a repo where one task legitimately spans several modules.

nodes.title: Concurrency bought a median 1.45x round speedup, not the 2x the pool size implies
nodes.body: On 134 rounds after the concurrent-dispatch change, speedup against a reconstructed serial round (serial = wall - union + sum of attempt intervals) has median 1.45, p25 1.21, p75 1.59, max 2.00; 71% of rounds are at least 1.30 and 10% are at most 1.02, i.e. no gain at all. Attempt-interval union covers only 0.56 of round wall (median), against 0.98 before, so the pool genuinely overlaps, but 44% of the round sits outside any attempt: planning (planMs is 0.27 of wall in rounds that plan), then promotion, guard and commit. The shortfall from 2.0 to 1.45 is that residual serial work, which no amount of candidate parallelism removes. Limitation: the serial counterfactual is arithmetic on ledger intervals, not a re-run, so it assumes the two attempts would have taken the same time dispatched one after the other - plausible only because they are near-equal in length (min/max duration ratio median 0.93).

nodes.title: Round wall time rose from 236s to 630s across the same change, so faster rounds meant a slower loop
nodes.body: Rounds with two candidates and wall above 5s after the change have median wall 630s; the 60 pre-change two-attempt rounds have median 236s. Both statements hold at once: per-round speedup improved to a 1.45 median while the median round got 2.7x longer in absolute terms, because attempts themselves grew (attemptMs median 618s) and work was reorganised into two-candidate rounds. Throughput per wall-clock hour therefore cannot be read off the speedup ratio; the honest denominator is tasks landed per hour, which nothing in this ledger computes. Limitation: pre and post differ in task mix, model and attempt deadline, so the 236-to-630 move is confounded - it is reported as a warning against citing 1.45 alone, not as a causal claim about parallelism.

nodes.title: An external replay study finds parallel wall clock bottoms out at N=4 and gets worse by N=16
nodes.body: worktree-fleet replays real commits as parallel agents through a tested merge queue over five Python histories (591 windows, 1328 tasks at N=16). Makespan in agent rounds divided by N: 0.59 at N=2, 0.44 at N=4, 0.44 at N=8, 0.49 at N=16, against 1.00 serial. Past N=8 every extra agent adds more redos than it saves rounds. Our configuration (cap 2) sits at the steep part of that curve, which is the only configuration this external evidence actually endorses. Limitation: wall clock is counted in agent rounds rather than seconds, a redo is charged a full round, and the agents replay human commits instead of reasoning, so the curve's shape may shift when generations differ in cost.

nodes.title: At 16 parallel agents 42.5% of first attempts are thrown away and only 13.7% touch code
nodes.body: Same study: first attempt discarded in 9.0/18.7/31.4/42.5% of tasks at N=2/4/8/16, and of those only 3.6/5.9/10.2/13.7% touched a .py line. The rest are changelogs, CI configs and lock files - 'files nobody would describe in a task'. Marking CHANGES*/CHANGELOG* as merge=union drops the totals to 6.4/12.3/21.9/30.5%. The mechanism is that conflict probability scales with files touched per change, and a handful of high-traffic housekeeping files dominate that count, so the cost of parallelism is set by repository hygiene rather than by task difficulty. Limitation: replay cherry-picks, so 'thrown away' means 'does not apply to the stale base'; a real agent from a stale base would instead collide later at merge time, making this a lower bound on real cost rather than a measurement of it.

nodes.title: Clean-merge-then-fail is 1.1% because 20 of 22 breakages need a file the pair never shared
nodes.body: Of 6,339 merge candidates the queue tested that real history never contained, 81 broke a test that passed on main and on the task's own commit: 1.1% at N=16 and 0.0/0.3/0.9% at N=2/4/8. Twenty of the 22 distinct causes were stale-base - a test-only commit landing before the code it tests, sharing no file - and one was a genuine interaction (more-itertools d17d077 chunked_even plus 6ccc5d7 docstring rewrite merged cleanly into a SyntaxError, an unterminated docstring). This is why file-overlap prediction cannot see the expensive class and why an executable gate is not optional. Limitation: one genuine interaction in a replayed corpus is a fact about these five histories, not a rate for independent agents, and the authors state replay cannot manufacture interactions that history lacked.

nodes.title: The only cheap conflict predictor degenerates into a serial scheduler at 0.97 of serial wall time
nodes.body: Given task text plus repository, a predictor that holds back tasks likely to overlap cuts thrown-away attempts from 42.5% to 1.0% at N=16 - and lands at wall-clock 0.97, i.e. it serialises nearly everything, because CHANGES.rst is touched by most changes so almost every pair is separated. Hiding the changelog from it gives 15.4% thrown away at 0.71 wall: better, but it then misses half the collisions, since the files that actually collide (uv.lock, .pre-commit-config.yaml, CI workflows, requirements/*.txt) are never named in a task. Oracle file knowledge reaches 0.4%/0.55 and oracle hunks 0.5%/0.43 - the ceiling, and unavailable before the run. Limitation: five repositories whose changelog convention is the mechanism; a monorepo without a CHANGES file would sit somewhere else on this curve, and nobody has measured where.

nodes.title: Two concurrent add+commit into one repository failed 29 of 30 attempts on the git index lock
nodes.body: I ran a probe on a scratch repository: pairs of processes each write a file, then run git add -A and git commit, concurrently. At N=2, 15 of 15 batches had at least one failed git command (29 failing commands of 30); at N=3 and N=4, 12 of 12 batches each. Every failure was fatal: Unable to create '.git/index.lock': File exists. Serial commits: 20 of 20 clean. git does not retry, and the failure exits 128. So any two writers to one checkout - two campaigns promoting, autopilot plus a human approval - race on a resource that no worktree isolates. Limitation: this is a synthetic repo with no backoff, and our promote-to-commit window is short (median 1.1s, p90 26.7s), so real exposure is the overlap of those windows, which I measured as 2 cross-campaign round overlaps in 227 rounds.

nodes.title: The second candidate is the only passing one in 9% of rounds, for 2x the attempt spend
nodes.body: Across 225 two-candidate rounds: both pass 83 (37%), a1 fails and a2 passes 21 (9%), a1 passes and a2 fails 30 (13%), both fail 91 (40%). The marginal value of the second slot is therefore 21/225 = 9% of rounds; in 37% it duplicates a candidate that already passed, and in 40% neither works. Duplicated second attempts account for $0.0112 of $0.1076 total two-candidate spend (10.4%) and 5.8 hours of agent wall time. Simultaneous failure in 40% of rounds also says the pair is not a hedge against flakiness - the candidates fail together, which is what a shared model and a shared brief predict. Limitation: score is binary 0/1 for all 452 attempts, so 'both pass' is an undifferentiated tie and the data cannot say whether the second candidate was ever better but merely unpreferred.

nodes.title: When both candidates pass, the tie-break is the attempt id, so a1 won 43 of 43 promotions
nodes.body: gate.rankAttempts sorts by score, then verifierOk, then id ascending. With a 0/1 verifier, two passing candidates are exactly tied and the comparator returns a1. In the ledger all 83 rounds where both candidates passed scored 1 and 1, and of the 43 that produced a named promotion, 43 promoted the a1 slot and 0 promoted a2 - despite a2 carrying the larger patch in 25 of those rounds. The practical consequence is that 'best of two' is lexicographic in a third of rounds, so the selection is not choosing quality at all there; it is choosing a filename. Limitation: this is a property of a binary gate plus a deterministic comparator, not of the design's intent; with a graded score or a cost tie-break the same code would decide differently, and I did not test that variant.

nodes.title: The repository carries 490 undeleted loom/* branches and 501 refs, growing with every attempt
nodes.body: git for-each-ref reports 501 refs, 490 of them refs/heads/loom/*, one per attempted candidate; no code path in src/ deletes a branch (no branch -D, no deleteBranch). Worktree directories are removed, branches are not. Creating a worktree still takes 0.44-0.97s on the real repo, so no slowdown is measurable yet. The risk is monotonic growth of refs and packed-refs (35KB now) inside a repository the loop rewrites for thousands of rounds, plus 490 names that make git branch output useless to a human reviewer trying to see what is in flight. Limitation: I did not measure worktree-add or gc cost as a function of ref count on this repo, so 'it will get slow' is an inference from 501 refs, not a measured curve.

nodes.title: Concurrent worktree creation never failed: 0 of 62 adds at N=2..32 with unique branch names
nodes.body: The failure the code guards against - prune deleting a sibling's admin directory mid-creation - did not reproduce: 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 simultaneous git worktree add -B with unique branch names gave 0 failures, wall 0.25/0.29/0.57/1.00/2.13s. The only failure I could force was a duplicate branch name ('b0 is already used by worktree at ...') at N>=4 when names were reused, which is a naming bug rather than a git race. Our 452 attempts used 452 distinct branch names and 452 distinct worktree paths, so that hazard is currently avoided by construction rather than by design. Limitation: a one-commit scratch repo on one filesystem; the real hazard window is a few milliseconds of gitdir-file creation and would need a much larger sample, or a slower disk, to hit.

nodes.title: A write through the junctioned node_modules landed in the shared repo tree and in no patch
nodes.body: linkDependencies makes worktree/node_modules a junction to repo/node_modules. I wrote a file through a worktree's junction; it appeared immediately at C:/Projects/RSI/node_modules/@deepseek-ai/probe.txt, so a candidate's filesystem write mutated the shared dependency tree. makePatch excludes node_modules by pathspec, which means the mutation is invisible to the patch, to the verifier diff and to any guard, and it persists into the next candidate and the next campaign. A dependency install, a lockfile rewrite or a tool cache write by any attempt edits state every other attempt reads, and nothing in the loop can detect it. Limitation: my probe was a plain file write, and I found no instance in the 437 artifact patches or in any ledger event where a candidate really modified the shared tree, so the exposure is demonstrated rather than observed.

nodes.title: The suite takes 246s alone and 358s with two running, so the verifier is a serial floor
nodes.body: In a worktree with a junctioned dependency tree, scripts/test-all.mjs (157 suites) takes 245.8s alone. Two concurrent runs in two worktrees: 358.0 and 358.3s. Four concurrent: 405.5 to 411.0s. Doubling the work costs 1.46x wall (capacity gain 1.37x) and quadrupling costs 1.67x, so contention is real but sublinear and there is a hard per-suite serial component. In the ledger, test-all as a guard has median 44.7s and max 79.4s over only 12 runs, while spec-level verifiers are 157ms median; the guard tail is what dominates a round that uses it. Limitation: one host with 32 logical CPUs and no CPU pinning, so a 4-core machine would degrade far more, and most real verifiers here are single-spec rather than the full suite.

nodes.title: Nine promotions were blocked by untracked files a human or a sibling agent had just written
nodes.body: applyPatch refuses to touch a dirty workspace: 9 checkpoint.raises with reason workspace-dirty, plus 2 more recorded in attempt text. The dominant cause is not a candidate: untracked research notes and specs written by a person or a sibling research agent into the shared checkout - loom-life2 '?? research/balance-2026-11.md', loom-tri13 '?? research/dag-2026-11.md', loom-plan2 '?? tests/ui/policy-visible.test.mjs'. Each becomes an anomaly checkpoint, so typing a scratch note into the repo stalls the autonomous loop until someone answers. One case was self-referential: loom-self3 r7a1 reported ' M src/exec/patch.js' and ' M src/runtime/round.js', i.e. it observed a live modification to its own apply path. Limitation: 9 instances over 69 campaigns, and authorship is inferred from path prefixes (research/, tests/ui/), not from any recorded writer identity, because the ledger does not record who wrote an untracked file.

nodes.title: One approved promotion committed a research note beside its code because commitWorkspace stages everything
nodes.body: commitWorkspace runs git add -A and then commits whatever is dirty. Of 71 promotion commits whose artifact patch still exists, 0 carried files absent from that patch - but the human-approved path behaves differently: 49942ea 'loom loom-tri13: apply approved promotion' committed research/dag-2026-11.md (49 lines changed) next to src/runtime/round.js, and no patch in loom-tri13/artifacts mentions research/ at all. Across all 114 loom commits it is the single commit not explained by its campaign's own patches. That is a demonstrated instance of a promotion sweeping another party's uncommitted work into a commit the loop then treats as its own landing. Limitation: n=1, it went through human approval rather than autopilot, and the swept file was an untracked note rather than another campaign's code, so it proves the mechanism and not a rate.

nodes.title: 63 campaigns share one workspace with no mutex, but only 4 rounds ever overlapped in time
nodes.body: 63 of 69 campaigns declare workspace C:/Projects/RSI, and 430 campaign pairs have overlapping time windows. Yet over 227 rounds with both start and finish, only 4 round pairs overlapped, 2 of them cross-campaign, and at most 2 rounds were ever in flight at once. runtime.tick() has no workspace mutex - it only skips a campaign that already has a round in flight - so the invariant is currently held by session.maxConcurrent defaulting to 2, a budget that one two-candidate round consumes entirely. Raise the cap, or make rounds shorter, and two campaigns will apply and commit into the same checkout concurrently, which my probe shows fails hard. Limitation: 227 rounds is a small sample, and round-window overlap understates risk because apply and commit occupy only the final seconds of a round while I measured overlap of whole rounds.

nodes.title: Campaigns are busy 99% of their own span, so removing human latency would not speed the loop
nodes.body: For 68 campaigns, the sum of round walls divided by first-to-last round span has median 0.99 (p25 0.98): the machine is essentially never idle waiting for anything. 50 checkpoints were raised, with raised-to-answered median 2,835s and p90 274,239s, totalling 924.5 cumulative hours of open-checkpoint time - yet that time is not lost throughput, because other campaigns kept running rounds throughout. End-to-end wall clock is therefore set by what happens inside a round (attempts plus the 44% residual), not by the human, which weakens the case for batching checkpoints as a latency win. Limitation: 'busy' means at least one round in flight in that campaign, which counts a round whose attempts are all dead as busy; 4 of 68 campaigns sit under 0.5, so the aggregate hides a stalled minority.

nodes.title: Best code judge averages 82% but drops to 62% on hard codegen and 43% for Claude-3.7
nodes.body: CodeJudgeBench (Jiang et al., arXiv:2507.10535) labels 5,352 candidate pairs from LiveCodeBench-v6 by unit-test execution and scores 26 judges on them. The best model, Gemini-2.5-Pro, averages 82.12%, but its hard-split code-generation accuracy is 62.24%, and Claude-3.7-Sonnet falls to 43.18% on the same hard split, below the 50% chance floor. Non-thinking judges sit at 52.9-59.1% overall (AceCodeRM-7B 52.92, Skywork-Critic-70B 55.98, Prometheus-14B 57.04) and near 50% on hard items. Any promotion gate that only ever sees hard, frontier-quality pairs is operating near noise rather than near 82%. Limitation: this is execution-free judging of competition-style problems, and the hard split is defined by judge consensus, so it is not a real-repository patch distribution.

nodes.title: A judge's accuracy is a property of the generator-judge pair, not a scalar of the judge
nodes.body: Table 7 of CodeJudgeBench (arXiv:2507.10535) uses a best-of-N protocol in which the judge must prefer the correct candidate over every incorrect one. Gemini-2.5-Pro scores 42.46% when the candidates were generated by Gemini-2.5-Pro, and 81.92% when the same judge scores candidates from Claude-3.7-Sonnet; Claude-3.7-Sonnet scores 29.85% and 46.00% on those same two pools. Judge capability is therefore not a number you can look up in a leaderboard: it is indexed by whose output is being judged, and the worst cell is judging your own family.
